metadata.title: U.S. semiconductor industry faces shortage of 157,000 workers by 2030

content.text:
The U.S. semiconductor industry faces a shortfall of between 127,000 and 157,000 workers by 2030, according to a new analysis conducted by the SEMI Foundation in collaboration with McKinsey & Company, as chipmakers including Samsung and Micron scale up domestic manufacturing to meet demand for artificial intelligence hardware.
Speaking with CNBC, Jon Taylor — executive vice president of Samsung's semiconductor operations in Austin, Texas — said the company is struggling to find enough qualified candidates. "We just don't see that there's enough technical people in the pipeline," Taylor said. Samsung expects its two new fabrication plants in Taylor, Texas — part of a $35 billion buildout — to create roughly 3,500 jobs, and the company is currently recruiting engineers, technicians, and supply chain workers.
According to CNBC, just 3% of U.S. engineering graduates go on to work in the semiconductor industry annually, and 73% of chip employers say they struggle significantly to fill engineering positions.
Micron is building the country's first advanced memory fabrication plant in Boise, Idaho, with another under construction in Clay, New York. SK Hynix's first U.S. footprint is a $4 billion memory-packaging facility taking shape at Purdue Research Park in West Lafayette, Indiana. That puts SK Hynix and Micron on a collision course as they vie for the same scarce domestic talent. "It's really the critical issue," SK Hynix CEO Kwak Noh-Jung told CNBC.
To bridge the gap, the SEMI Foundation launched the first four Regional Nodes of the National Network for Microelectronics Education in May, a workforce initiative funded by the National Science Foundation in partnership with the U.S. Department of Commerce. The network connects more than 325 organizations — including K-12 districts, colleges, and semiconductor employers — across four regional hubs led by the Arizona Commerce Authority, Boise State University, NY Creates, and the University of Texas at Austin. Each node may receive up to $20 million over five years, the SEMI Foundation said.
"Building the semiconductor workforce our country needs isn't something any one company or institution can do alone," April Arnzen, executive vice president and chief people officer at Micron Technology, said in a statement.
As the gap between available workers and open roles has widened, chipmakers and universities have moved to build domestic pipelines. Purdue University, which rolled out a slate of semiconductor degree programs in 2022, now counts roughly 2,500 students taking chip-related coursework each term. Arizona State University turned a shuttered Motorola fab into the MacroTechnology Works cleanroom training center, a project backed by a $200 million investment from Applied Materials. Since the CHIPS Act's passage in 2022, upward of 80 community colleges have started or grown semiconductor programs, relying in part on a $200 million federal workforce fund.
